evidence: Read CONTEXT.txt whole first (the "Before you begin" section; the shared context carries the S23, S24 and S25 drafts together), then DRAFT.txt, SOURCE.txt and the_change. The draft, "Make sure you're in a safe place to do this.", occurs once in the context, as the opening sentence of the safety paragraph, and is exactly the sentence the_change names (the "samples cm and co" provenance is the claim in the_change; the samples are not among my files). It replaces "Put yourself in a place where you can safely do this." with a plain imperative doing the same job in the same slot. Meaning: SOURCE's published sentence asks for a physically secure place with no driving, water, machinery or anyone needing your supervision. The draft keeps the safe place, and the next sentence, which the change leaves alone, carries the hazards ("Don't do this if you're driving, in the water, operating machinery, or otherwise need to be attending to yourself or other people."), so nothing is lost and no claim, hedge or fact is added; that next sentence also makes "safe" physical, so it does not drift into the therapy sense of a safe place. "This" is anchored by "spend on this" and "do this on a problem" in the paragraph before. Read in place there is no seam, no summary, no wrapper and no change of writer: same register as the sentences on either side. Tell rows: T02 is the one row I find actually happening, and only in the inherited paragraph: the safety paragraph is a run of commands and conditions that each do one job and hand off (be somewhere safe; not if driving; if intoxicated get support; if already open use the later section). I judge it justified: they are separate safety rules for separate situations, the replaced sentence was already a command in this slot, and the draft swaps one command for one command and adds none. T26: the previous paragraph ends "Make sure you're leaving some time at the end..." and "make sure you can change state" follows two paragraphs later, so the frame is heard three times in the section; I judge it absent because "make sure you're" is an ordinary checklist frame, not a distinctive phrase, the other two are unchanged sentences already in the section, and the parallel marks a list of preparations (an editor might vary the verb, but it is not a seam). T22: a bare imperative, but its reasons arrive in the next sentence. T06, T10, T19: no vague abstraction, permission packaging or announcement. T15: the draft is more ordinary than the words it replaces, not a rarer synonym. All other T and C rows absent: no first-person stake, scene, image, colon, closer, summary, tic word, kid-naming, invented fact or study claim, and one sentence in the same place, so nothing is moved. Linter: "D9 follows the source order" is a paragraph-structure flag, and a one-sentence swap in place cannot reorder anything; accepted. "E36/E41 heavy second person" (10.0 you per 100 words) is one "you're" in a ten-word sentence; the guide is addressed to you throughout and the sentence it replaces had two second-person words in eleven (yourself, you), so the draft is lighter; accepted.
